problem: The answer picks the NodeMCU because its average is about 2.69 mA and claims it can run a year on two AA cells. The arithmetic contradicts the requirement: 2.69 mA for 8760 h is about 23,600 mA·h, while two AA alkaline cells in series store only about 2500 mA·h, so the node would last about 2500 ÷ 2.69 ≈ 930 h ≈ 39 days, not a year.
fix: Keep the NodeMCU as the choice, but add the check: to last one year on two AA cells the average current must be below about 2500 mA·h ÷ 8760 h ≈ 0.29 mA. At 2.69 mA the cells last only about 39 days, so the sleep interval must be lengthened (or a larger cell used) before the design meets the one-year target.

problem: The high threshold is given as the general CMOS rule 0.7 × VDD = 2.31 V. The ESP8266 datasheet value is VIH = 0.75 × VDD = 2.475 V. The conclusion is unchanged, but a student may quote the wrong threshold for this chip.
fix: Say: the datasheet high threshold is about 0.75 × 3.3 V = 2.48 V (the 0.7 × VDD = 2.31 V rule is a common CMOS approximation), so 3.0 V is still a safe logic 1 and is below the 3.3 V supply.

problem: The 20 µA deep-sleep figure is for the ESP8266 chip alone. On a stock NodeMCU the 3.3 V regulator and the USB-to-serial chip keep drawing, so the measured board current in deep sleep is roughly a milliamp, not 20 µA. The worked example silently treats a NodeMCU as if it were a bare chip.
fix: Add one line: the 20 µA is the chip figure; the regulator and USB-to-serial chip on a NodeMCU add leakage, so a real board sleeps at about a milliamp unless those parts are removed or the bare module is used. Say the worked example uses the chip figure.

fix: Write: some syllabi also list the Cubieboard in this group, another Allwinner-based Linux board, but its GPIO comes out on pin headers rather than an Uno-layout shield socket.
